 "This brass compass is an example of a 'magnetic compass' made popular in the 18th century. A magnetic compass works by aligning itself with the Earth's magnetic field, which is generated by the movement of molten iron in the Earth's core. The compass contains a tiny bar magnet, which is suspended inside a wooden or ivory casing. The magnet is attached to a pivot, allowing it to rotate freely. When the compass is held near a magnetically susceptible material, such as a piece of iron or a lodestone, it will align itself with the magnetic field of that material. The compass needle will then point towards the magnetic North Pole, allowing navigators to determine their direction. In the case of the Earth's magnetic field, the compass needle points towards the North Magnetic Pole, which is located in northern Canada." A museum note, describing the working of a brass compass. It provides details about how the magnetic compass works, describing the movement of the Earth's core and the way the compass needle aligns with it.
A museum note describing how a brass compass works: "This brass compass is an example of a 'magnetic compass' made popular in the 18th century. A magnetic compass works by aligning itself with the Earth's magnetic field, which is generated by the movement of molten iron in the Earth's core. The compass contains a tiny bar magnet, which is suspended inside a wooden or ivory casing. The magnet is attached to a pivot, allowing it to rotate freely. When the compass is held near a magnetically susceptible material, such as a piece of iron or a lodestone, it will align itself with the magnetic field of that material. The compass needle will then point towards the magnetic North Pole, allowing navigators to determine their direction. In the case of the Earth's magnetic field, the compass needle points towards the North Magnetic Pole, which is located in northern Canada." A museum note, describing
